newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: Venezuela bolivar ends firmer on new forex rules.
newsitem.headline: Venezuela bolivar ends firmer on new forex rules.

text.p: The Venezuelan bolivar closed firmer at 494.50/495.50 per dollar Monday as the market reacted to new foreign currency trading rules and an increase in commercial bank's reserve requirement, traders said.
The bolivar closed at 495.50/496.50 Friday, from 496.50/497.50 Thursday.

The announcement Monday that the Central Bank was raising commercial banks' reserve requirement from 15 to 17 percent from Aug 11 saw many banks sell dollars to improve their local currency positions, traders said.

Foreign currency trading was also affected by a new measure which placed limits on interbank foreign exchange trading, reclassifying a number of brokerages and institutions previously considered as end clients.

Under foreign currency trading regulations, 67 percent of all foreign currency trading carried out by commercial banks must be with final clients and only 33 percent can be carried out on the interbank market.
Traders said the new measure, which took effect Monday, will reduce currency volatility.
"The Central Bank now has a lot more control," one said.

The announcement that the foreign exchange bands monthly depreciation rate had been reduced to 1.16 percent from 1.32 percent had also sent a message of stability to the market which had been concerned by the accelerated depreciation of the bolivar last month, traders said.
The bolivar depreciated by nearly two percent in July compared to just 2.5 percent over the first half of the year.

In an interview with Reuters during a visit to Brazil Monday, Central Bank President Antonio Casas Gonzalez stressed that there was no need for concern over recent currency movements and stressed that the Bank's currency policy had not changed.
"What we want is exchange stability and we want it without the general overvaluation and we want it within the targets that we've set out with inflation," Casas said.

Venezuela's foreign exchange market is unusual in that the Central Bank is its largest single supplier of dollars, which blurs the difference between the Central Bank supplying liquidity and intervening.
